Appendix A Calculation of the gradient of the free energy

In order to calculate the derivatives of ℱH​[ℋ]\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}], it is convenient to work with normal coordinates. The quantum statistical average of an operator that exclusively depends on atomic positions can be calculated in normal coordinates applying the change of variables defined in Eq. (13) to Eq. (18), namely

tr⁡[ρℋ​O]=∫d​𝐪​O​(…,Reqs​α+∑μ=13​N1Ms​ϵμ​ℋs​α​qμ,…)​ρℋ​(𝐪),\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}O]=\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{q}O(\dots,R_{{\rm eq}}^{s\alpha}+\sum_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}q_{\mu},\dots)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q}), (48)

where 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a general configuration of the normal coordinates and ρℋ​(𝐪)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q}) is the probability to find the system in the configuration 𝐪\mathbf{q}. In normal coordinates, ρℋ​(𝐪)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q}) is nothing but a product of Gaussians [73]:

ρℋ​(𝐪)=∏μ=13​N1aμ​ℋ​2​π​e−qμ22​aμ​ℋ2.\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q})=\prod_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{q^{2}_{\mu}}{2a^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}}. (49)

If we make use of the yμ=qμ/aμ​ℋy_{\mu}=q_{\mu}/a_{\mu\mathcal{H}} change of variables, the integral can be written as

tr⁡[ρℋ​O]\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}O] =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐲​O​(…,Reqs​α+∑μ=13​N1Ms​ϵμ​ℋs​α​aμ​ℋ​yμ,…)\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}O(\dots,R_{{\rm eq}}^{s\alpha}+\sum_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}y_{\mu},\dots) (50)
×∏μ=13​N12​π​e−yμ22,\displaystyle\times\prod_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{y^{2}_{\mu}}{2}},

where 𝐲\mathbf{y} represents all the set of yμy_{\mu}’s. Writing the quantum statistical average in this way, the exponential part becomes independent of phonon frequencies, polarizations vectors and equilibrium positions.

The only non analytic part in the calculation of ℱH​[ℋ]=Fℋ+tr⁡[ρℋ​(V−𝒱)]\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]=F_{\mathcal{H}}+\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(V-\mathcal{V})] is the quantum statistical average of the potential, the tr⁡[ρℋ​V]\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V] term. The analytic expression of FℋF_{\mathcal{H}} is given in Eq. (19) and

tr⁡[ρℋ​𝒱]=∑μ=13​N12​ωμ​ℋ2​aμ​ℋ2.\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{V}]=\sum_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{2}\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}a^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}. (51)

Before we demonstrate Eqs. (21) and (22), we also would like to note the following analytical relation involving the 𝐟ℋ​(𝐑)\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}) harmonic forces:

∫d​𝐑​fℋs​α​(𝐑)​(Rt​β−Reqt​β)​ρℋ​(𝐑)=\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}f^{s\alpha}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})(R^{t\beta}-R^{t\beta}_{\mathrm{eq}})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})=
−∑μ=13​NMsMtϵμ​ℋs​αϵμ​ℋt​βω2μ​ℋa2μ​ℋ.\displaystyle\ \ \ -\sum_{\mu=1}^{3N}\sqrt{\frac{M_{s}}{M_{t}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}a^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}. (52)

First of all, if we write tr⁡[ρℋ​V]\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V] as in Eq. (50), it is easy to observe that

∇𝐑eqℱH[ℋ]=∇𝐑eqtr[ρℋV]=−∫d𝐑𝐟(𝐑)ρℋ(𝐑).\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\mathbf{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}}\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]=\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\mathbf{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}}\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V]=-\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{R})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}). (53)

Noting that ∫d​𝐑𝐟ℋ​(𝐑)​ρℋ​(𝐑)=0\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{f}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})=0, we recover Eq. (21).

Secondly, we calculate ∇ΦℱH​[ℋ]\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}] using the chain rule as

∇ΦℱH​[ℋ]=∑μ∂ℱH​[ℋ]∂aμ​ℋ​∇Φaμ​ℋ+∑μ​s​α∂ℱH​[ℋ]∂ϵμ​ℋs​α​∇Φϵμ​ℋs​α.\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]=\sum_{\mu}\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}+\sum_{\mu s\alpha}\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]}{\partial\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}. (54)

The partial derivative with respect to the polarization vectors is easily obtained writing again tr⁡[ρℋ​V]\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V] as in Eq. (50). In particular,

∂ℱH​[ℋ]∂ϵμ​ℋs​α\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]}{\partial\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}} =\displaystyle= ∂tr⁡[ρℋ​V]∂ϵμ​ℋs​α=−∑t​βMtMsϵμ​ℋt​β\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V]}{\partial\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}=-\sum_{t\beta}\sqrt{\frac{M_{t}}{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta} (55)
×\displaystyle\times ∫d​𝐑​fs​α​(𝐑)​(Rt​β−Reqt​β)​ρℋ​(𝐑).\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}f^{s\alpha}(\mathbf{R})(R^{t\beta}-R^{t\beta}_{\mathrm{eq}})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}).

Making use of Eq. (52) we can write

∂ℱH​[ℋ]∂ϵμ​ℋs​α=ϵμ​ℋs​α​ωμ​ℋ2​aμ​ℋ2−∑t​βMtMs​ϵμ​ℋt​β\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]}{\partial\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}=\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}a^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}-\sum_{t\beta}\sqrt{\frac{M_{t}}{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}
×∫d​𝐑​[fs​α​(𝐑)−fℋs​α​(𝐑)]​(Rt​β−Reqt​β)​ρℋ​(𝐑).\displaystyle\ \ \times\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}[f^{s\alpha}(\mathbf{R})-f^{s\alpha}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})](R^{t\beta}-R^{t\beta}_{\mathrm{eq}})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}). (56)

On the other hand,

∂ℱH​[ℋ]∂aμ​ℋ=∂(Fℋ−tr⁡[ρℋ​𝒱])∂aμ​ℋ+∂tr⁡[ρℋ​V]∂aμ​ℋ\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}]}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}=\frac{\partial\left(F_{\mathcal{H}}-\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{V}]\right)}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}+\frac{\partial\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V]}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}} (57)

It is straightforward to demonstrate that

∂tr⁡[ρℋ​V]∂aμ​ℋ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V]}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}} =\displaystyle= −∑s​t​α​βMtMsϵμ​ℋs​αϵμ​ℋt​β1aμ​ℋ\displaystyle-\sum_{st\alpha\beta}\sqrt{\frac{M_{t}}{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}\frac{1}{a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}} (58)
×\displaystyle\times ∫d​𝐑​fs​α​(𝐑)​(Rt​β−Reqt​β)​ρℋ​(𝐑)\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}f^{s\alpha}(\mathbf{R})(R^{t\beta}-R^{t\beta}_{\mathrm{eq}})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})

if Eq. (50) is used to write the quantum statistical average. Using Eq. (52) the equation above can be rewritten as

∂tr⁡[ρℋ​V]∂aμ​ℋ=ωμ​ℋ2​aμ​ℋ−∑s​t​α​βMtMs​ϵμ​ℋs​α​ϵμ​ℋt​β​1aμ​ℋ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}V]}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}=\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}-\sum_{st\alpha\beta}\sqrt{\frac{M_{t}}{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}\frac{1}{a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}
×∫d​𝐑​[fs​α​(𝐑)−fℋs​α​(𝐑)]​(Rt​β−Reqt​β)​ρℋ​(𝐑).\displaystyle\times\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{R}[f^{s\alpha}(\mathbf{R})-f^{s\alpha}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R})](R^{t\beta}-R^{t\beta}_{\mathrm{eq}})\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}). (59)

Finally, plugging Eqs. (59) and (56) into Eq. (54), and noting that

∂(Fℋ−tr⁡[ρℋ​𝒱])∂aμ​ℋ+ωμ​ℋ2​aμ​ℋ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\left(F_{\mathcal{H}}-\mathrm{tr}[\rho_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{V}]\right)}{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}+\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}} =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 (60)
∑s​αϵμ​ℋs​α​∇Φϵμ​ℋs​α\displaystyle\sum_{s\alpha}\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (61)

it is straightforward to obtain the expression for ∇ΦℱH​[ℋ]\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}] given in Eq. (22).

The only elements contributing to ∇ΦℱH​[ℋ]\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\mathcal{F}_{H}[\mathcal{H}] that have not been specified yet are ∇Φaμ​ℋ\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}} and ∇Φϵμ​ℋs​α\boldsymbol{\nabla}_{\Phi}\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}. Considering how eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix are modified when the matrix itself is varied, we can get the following expressions for the components of these gradients:

∂aμ​ℋ∂Φs​tα​β\displaystyle\frac{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}{\partial\Phi^{\alpha\beta}_{st}} =\displaystyle= ∂aμ​ℋ∂ωμ​ℋ​12​ωμ​ℋ​ϵμ​ℋs​α​ϵμ​ℋt​βMs​Mt\displaystyle\frac{\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}{\partial\omega_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}\frac{1}{2\omega_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}\frac{\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}}{\sqrt{M_{s}M_{t}}} (62)
∂ϵμ​ℋs​α∂Φk​tγ​β\displaystyle\frac{\partial\epsilon^{s\alpha}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}}{\partial\Phi^{\gamma\beta}_{kt}} =\displaystyle= ∑ν,ν≠μϵν​ℋk​γ​ϵμ​ℋt​βMk​Mt​(ωμ​ℋ2−ων​ℋ2)​ϵν​ℋs​α.\displaystyle\sum_{\nu,\nu\neq\mu}\frac{\epsilon_{\nu\mathcal{H}}^{k\gamma}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{t\beta}}{\sqrt{M_{k}M_{t}}(\omega^{2}_{\mu\mathcal{H}}-\omega^{2}_{\nu\mathcal{H}})}\epsilon_{\nu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}. (63)

The ∂aμ​ℋ/∂ωμ​ℋ\partial a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}/\partial\omega_{\mu\mathcal{H}} derivative in Eq. (62) can be obtained from Eq. (17).

Appendix B Symmetrization and reduction of the basis for the force-constants matrix

In order to apply S^\hat{S} and time-reversal symmetries to the {𝒢(ns)​(m)}m=1,…,(3​n)2​N1​N2​N3\{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(m)\}_{m=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}N_{1}N_{2}N_{3}} basis, it is convenient to to work in the unit-cell phonon-momentum 𝐪\mathbf{q} space. This is so because any Φ\Phi force-constants matrix of this vector space respects translational symmetries and, thus, its Fourier transform can be labeled with a single 𝐪\mathbf{q} vector of the 1BZ of the unit cell. The number of 𝐪\mathbf{q} points in the 1BZ is determined by the supercell size. A N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} supercell means a N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} phonon-momentum grid in the 1BZ of the unit cell. The Fourier components of the real-space force-constants matrix of the supercell Φ\Phi are labeled as Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}). Each Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}) is a 3​n×3​n3n\times 3n Hermitian matrix. Therefore, in practice we do not work with the vector space defined by the {𝒢(ns)​(m)}m=1,…,(3​n)2​N1​N2​N3\{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(m)\}_{m=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}N_{1}N_{2}N_{3}} basis, but with the vector space formed by the 3​n×3​n3n\times 3n Hermitian matrices. The dimension of this vector space is (3​n)2(3n)^{2} and let {𝒢¯(ns)​(σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} be an orthonormal basis of it. The elements of the basis satisfy the orthonormality condition defined in Eq. (30). Therefore, any Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}) can be decomposed in this basis as

Φ⁡(𝐪)=∑σ=1(3​n)2c(ns)​(𝐪,σ)​𝒢¯(ns)​(σ),\Phi(\mathbf{q})=\sum_{\sigma=1}^{(3n)^{2}}c_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma), (64)

where the c(ns)​(𝐪,σ)c_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma) coefficients determine the value of Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}).

Any Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}) matrix described in the {𝒢¯(ns)​(σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} basis as in Eq. (64) transforms under the symmetry operations S^\hat{S} of the space group as

Φ⁡(S​𝐪)=TS^​(𝐪)​Φ​(𝐪)​TS^†​(𝐪),\Phi(S\mathbf{q})=T_{\hat{S}}(\mathbf{q})\Phi(\mathbf{q})T_{\hat{S}}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q}), (65)

where the unitary TS^​(𝐪)T_{\hat{S}}(\mathbf{q}) matrices are given in Refs. 51, 74, 75. Eq. (65) shows that many of the 𝐪\mathbf{q} points in the N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} mesh are equivalent by symmetry since the force-constants matrices at S​𝐪S\mathbf{q} points of the 1BZ are related by symmetry to the force-constants matrix at 𝐪\mathbf{q}. The set of symmetry related S​𝐪S\mathbf{q} points is named as the star of 𝐪\mathbf{q} and we denote it as {𝐪∗}\{\mathbf{q}^{*}\}. The 𝐪\mathbf{q} points not related by Eq. (65) form the irreducible Brillouin zone (IBZ). Therefore, we can restrict the Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}) Fourier-components of the supercell force-constants matrix at the 𝐪\mathbf{q} points in the IBZ. Indeed, all the N1×N2×N3N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} Φ⁡(𝐪)\Phi(\mathbf{q}) matrices can be generated by symmetry using Eq. (65).

Eq. (65) can be used to symmetrize the elements of the {𝒢¯(ns)​(σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} basis with respect to the S^\hat{S} operations and time-reversal. For instance, if

S𝐪​𝐪=𝐪+𝐆𝐪S_{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{q}} (66)

or

S−𝐪​𝐪=−𝐪+𝐆−𝐪,S_{-\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{q}+\mathbf{G}_{-\mathbf{q}}, (67)

we can use the S^𝐪\hat{S}_{\mathbf{q}} and S^−𝐪\hat{S}_{-\mathbf{q}} symmetry operations to symmetrize the basis. The S^𝐪\hat{S}_{\mathbf{q}} symmetry operations form the so-called small group of 𝐪\mathbf{q}. The S^−𝐪\hat{S}_{-\mathbf{q}} operations can be used to symmetrize the basis because of time-reversal symmetry. From Eq. (65) it is straightforward to observe that the elements of the basis can be symmetrized as

𝒢¯(s)​(𝐪,σ)=1NS𝐪​∑S^𝐪TS^𝐪†​(𝐪)​𝒢¯(ns)​(σ)​TS^𝐪​(𝐪)\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(s)}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)=\frac{1}{N_{S_{\mathbf{q}}}}\sum_{\hat{S}_{\mathbf{q}}}T_{\hat{S}_{\mathbf{q}}}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q})\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma)T_{\hat{S}_{\mathbf{q}}}(\mathbf{q})
+1NS−𝐪∑S^−𝐪TS^−𝐪†(𝐪)𝒢¯(ns)∗(σ)TS^−𝐪(𝐪),\displaystyle\ \ \ \ +\frac{1}{N_{S_{-\mathbf{q}}}}\sum_{\hat{S}_{-\mathbf{q}}}T_{\hat{S}_{-\mathbf{q}}}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{q})\bar{\mathcal{G}}^{*}_{\mathrm{(ns)}}(\sigma)T_{\hat{S}_{-\mathbf{q}}}(\mathbf{q}), (68)

where NS𝐪N_{S_{\mathbf{q}}} is the number symmetry operations in the small group of 𝐪\mathbf{q} and NS−𝐪N_{S_{-\mathbf{q}}} the number of symmetry operations satisfying Eq. (67). We perform this symmetrization at each 𝐪∈\mathbf{q}\in IBZ. The {𝒢¯(s)​(𝐪,σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(s)}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} basis becomes overcomplete after the symmetrization. We reduce the basis applying a Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization procedure. We label the set of matrices that form the basis of the symmetrized subspace as {𝒢¯​(𝐪,σ)}σ=1,…,Nr​(𝐪)\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,N_{r}(\mathbf{q})}, Nr​(𝐪)N_{r}(\mathbf{q}) being the dimension of the subspace for 𝐪∈\mathbf{q}\in IBZ.

In this framework, it is also easy to impose the acoustic sum rule (ASR) as among the 𝒢¯(s)​(Γ,σ)\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(s)}}(\Gamma,\sigma) matrices there must exist three translation generators, one for each Cartesian direction: 𝒢tx\mathcal{G}_{t}^{x}, 𝒢ty\mathcal{G}_{t}^{y} and 𝒢tz\mathcal{G}_{t}^{z}. According to the ASR, the translation vectors must be eigenvectors of the force-constants matrix at Γ\Gamma with vanishing eigenvalue. In order to impose this property, we redefine all the generators at Γ\Gamma according to the

𝒢¯ASR​(Γ,σ)=(𝕀−𝒢t)​𝒢¯(s)​(Γ,σ)​(𝕀−𝒢t)\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{ASR}}(\Gamma,\sigma)=(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{G}_{t})\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(s)}}(\Gamma,\sigma)(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{G}_{t}) (69)

projection, where 𝕀\mathbb{I} is the identity matrix and 𝒢t=𝒢tx+𝒢ty+𝒢tz\mathcal{G}_{t}=\mathcal{G}_{t}^{x}+\mathcal{G}_{t}^{y}+\mathcal{G}_{t}^{z}. Then, instead of performing the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization in the {𝒢¯(s)​(Γ,σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{(s)}}(\Gamma,\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} basis, we perform it in the {𝒢¯ASR​(Γ,σ)}σ=1,…,(3​n)2\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{ASR}}(\Gamma,\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,(3n)^{2}} one. This procedure gives us the {𝒢¯​(Γ,σ)}σ=1,…,Nr​(𝚪)\{\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\Gamma,\sigma)\}_{\sigma=1,\dots,N_{r}(\mathbf{\Gamma})} basis of the symmetric subspace at Γ\Gamma.

Once the symmetry reduced basis is found for all 𝐪∈\mathbf{q}\in IBZ, we decompose the initial force-constants matrix Φ⁡(0)\Phi(0) in the basis. In order to decompose it, it is sufficient to decompose the Fourier transformed force-constants matrices at 𝐪∈\mathbf{q}\in IBZ. The decomposition of each of these matrices is given as

Φ⁡(𝐪,0)=∑σ=1Nr​(𝐪)c0​(𝐪,σ)​𝒢¯​(𝐪,σ),\Phi(\mathbf{q},0)=\sum_{\sigma=1}^{N_{r}(\mathbf{q})}c_{0}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma), (70)

where the c0​(𝐪,σ)c_{0}(\mathbf{q},\sigma) coefficients can be obtain from the

c0​(𝐪,σ)=⟨Φ⁡(𝐪,0),𝒢¯​(𝐪,σ)⟩c_{0}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)=\langle\Phi(\mathbf{q},0),\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\rangle (71)

scalar product. The scalar product in Eq. (71) is defined in Eq. (29) though, in this case, the sum over atom indices is limited to the unit cell. It is clear that the total number of coefficients needed to determine Φ⁡(0)\Phi(0), or in general any Φ⁡(j)\Phi(j), is NR=∑𝐪∈IBZNr​(𝐪)N_{R}=\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathrm{IBZ}}N_{r}(\mathbf{q}).

Finally, in order to obtain Eq. (32), we need to Fourier transform to real space the 𝒢¯​(𝐪,σ)\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q},\sigma) matrices. The 𝒢¯​(𝐪′,σ)\bar{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q}^{\prime},\sigma) matrices for all 𝐪′∈{𝐪∗}\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\in\{\mathbf{q}^{*}\} can be obtained using Eq. (65). The

𝒢s​tα​β​(𝐪,σ)=1Nq​∑𝐪′∈{𝐪∗}𝒢¯s¯​t¯α​β​(𝐪′,σ)​ei​𝐪′​(𝐑s​s¯−𝐑t​t¯)\mathcal{G}_{st}^{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)=\frac{1}{N_{q}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\in\{\mathbf{q}^{*}\}}\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{\bar{s}\bar{t}}^{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q}^{\prime},\sigma)e^{i\mathbf{q}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}_{s\bar{s}}-\mathbf{R}_{t\bar{t}})} (72)

Fourier transform gives us the value of the matrix in real space. In Eq. (72) Nq=N1×N2×N3N_{q}=N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{3} is the total number of 𝐪\mathbf{q} points in the 1BZ and 𝐑s​s¯\mathbf{R}_{s\bar{s}} is the lattice vector that connects the ss-th atom of the supercell with the equivalent atom s¯\bar{s} in the unit cell, 𝐑s​s¯=𝐑eqs−𝐑eqs¯\mathbf{R}_{s\bar{s}}=\mathbf{R}^{s}_{{\rm eq}}-\mathbf{R}^{\bar{s}}_{{\rm eq}}. Note that 𝒢s​tα​β​(𝐪,σ)\mathcal{G}_{st}^{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q},\sigma) denotes an element of the symmetrized basis in real space and that 𝐪,σ\mathbf{q},\sigma is nothing but the label of a matrix in the basis. Moreover, as for 𝐪′∈{𝐪∗}\mathbf{q}^{\prime}\in\{\mathbf{q}^{*}\} c0​(𝐪′,σ)=c0​(𝐪,σ)c_{0}(\mathbf{q}^{\prime},\sigma)=c_{0}(\mathbf{q},\sigma), the Φ⁡(0)\Phi(0) force-constants matrix in real space can be calculated as

Φs​tα​β​(0)=∑𝐪∈IBZ∑σ=1Nr​(𝐪)c0​(𝐪,σ)​𝒢s​tα​β​(𝐪,σ).\Phi_{st}^{\alpha\beta}(0)=\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathrm{IBZ}}\sum_{\sigma=1}^{N_{r}(\mathbf{q})}c_{0}(\mathbf{q},\sigma)\mathcal{G}_{st}^{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q},\sigma). (73)

Simplifying the notation as m≡𝐪,σm\equiv\mathbf{q},\sigma we get

Φ⁡(0)=∑m=1NRc0​(m)​𝒢​(m),\Phi(0)=\sum_{m=1}^{N_{R}}c_{0}(m)\mathcal{G}(m), (74)

where the sum runs over the NRN_{R} different coefficients. Obviously at CG step jj Eq. (74) holds as in Eq. (32).

Appendix C Creating the set of ionic configurations

In order to create the {𝐑I}I=1,…,Nc\{\mathbf{R}_{I}\}_{I=1,\dots,N_{c}} set of ionic configurations according to the probability distribution ρℋ​(𝐑)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{R}), we take advantage of the Gaussian character of ρℋ​(𝐪)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q}) (see Eq. (49)). First of all, a set of {yμ​I}I=1,…,Nc\{y_{\mu I}\}_{I=1,\dots,N_{c}} configurations is created. Each yμ​Iy_{\mu I} is a random number created according to a purely Gaussian distribution. Then, we multiply each yμ​Iy_{\mu I} by the corresponding aμ​ℋa_{\mu\mathcal{H}} normal length. This operation gives us a set of configurations for the normal coordinates described by the ρℋ​(𝐪)\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathbf{q}) probability distribution: {qμ​I=aμ​ℋyμ​I}I=1,…,Nc\{q_{\mu I}=a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}y_{\mu I}\}_{I=1,\dots,N_{c}}. From Eq. (13), these normal coordinates define a set of configurations for the ionic positions {𝐑I}I=1,…,Nc\{\mathbf{R}_{I}\}_{I=1,\dots,N_{c}}, where each component is given as

RIs​α=Reqs​α+∑μ=13​N1Ms​ϵμ​ℋs​α​aμ​ℋ​yμ​I.R^{s\alpha}_{I}=R_{{\rm eq}}^{s\alpha}+\sum_{\mu=1}^{3N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{s}}}\epsilon_{\mu\mathcal{H}}^{s\alpha}a_{\mu\mathcal{H}}y_{\mu I}. (75)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
